_README: Vulnerability library for Report Generator. This file is the library: the app
reads it and the library editor writes it. vuln_library.json at the repository
root is an untracked local backup that no code references.
Edit through the library editor rather than by hand where possible. It
validates the whole document before replacing this file, because the library
is loaded at import time and a malformed file stops the app from starting.
Fragments are pre-converted. The app performs NO HTML parsing at runtime.
requires_tester_input=true means the entry contains placeholder text that
MUST be replaced before the report is complete. The review panel flags
those fragments until the tester has edited them.
Rich text is stored as runs: [{text, bold?, italic?, underline?}].

runs.text:
The model, while responding to specific topic queries, was found to generate inaccurate or misleading information. Despite being trained to process and evaluate specific tasks, it produced response misinterpreted data or made wrong assumptions. This could lead to poor decision making, potentially resulting in incorrect assessments, underwriting decisions or financial miscalculations. This dissemination of inaccurate information could expose the system to operational, compliance, and reputational risks, as users may rely on the model’s output for critical financial decisions without verifying the data.

(insert additional description for the vulnerability)
Reference: https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm092025-misinformation/
Improve the model’s accuracy and reliability through enhanced training and validation process.
Browse to the assistant page as a standard user.
Submit the crafted prompt in the chat box.
Compare the assistant answer against the account summary page.
Send POST /v1/assistant/query with the crafted prompt.
Inspect the JSON response body.
Compare the returned figure against GET /v1/accounts/{id}.

An API management interface is publicly accessible without proper authentication or access restrictions. This interface typically provides detailed information about API endpoints and may allow administrative actions such as configuration changes or key management. Exposing this functionality can enable attackers to gather intelligence about the system, identify potential vulnerabilities, and perform unauthorized operations. This significantly increases the risk of data leakage, API abuse, and compromise of backend services.
Limit access to the API management interface to internal networks or trusted IP ranges.
Enforce strong authentication for all users accessing the interface.
Ensure no credentials, tokens, or secrets are exposed through the interface.
Do not expose administrative or management portals to the internet unless absolutely necessary.

The application’s input fields have the autocomplete attribute enabled, allowing browsers to store and automatically populate sensitive information such as usernames, passwords, and personal data. While convenient for users, this feature increases the risk of credential theft if the device is compromised or shared, as stored values can be accessed by attackers or malicious software.
Set autocomplete="off" or autocomplete="new-password" for fields like login credentials, payment details, and personal information.
Ensure password fields use type="password" and are not cached by the browser.
Do not use incremental integer IDs so that IDs cannot be predicted.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

The application is vulnerable due to a broken authentication mechanism. The application was unable to perform the verification on the requests. During testing, authentication bearer or authentication token can be omitted, and users will receive a similar response as if they are authenticated. This vulnerability allows unauthorized users to update or tamper fields without proper authentication or authorization checks. This can lead to unauthorized modifications of policy details, resulting in potential data breaches, fraud, and financial loss. Attackers often target outdated components with publicly available exploits, which could lead to data breaches, privilege escalation, or complete system compromise depending on the role of the outdated technology.

(insert additional description for the vulnerability)
Implement Authorization Checks: Ensure that only authorized users can perform sensitive actions by validating user permissions on the server side.
Use Bearer Tokens: Secure API endpoints with Authorization Bearer Tokens to authenticate and authorize users.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

Unless directed otherwise, browsers may store a local cached copy of content received from web servers. Some browsers, including Internet Explorer, cache content accessed via HTTPS. If sensitive information in application responses is stored in the local cache, then this may be retrieved by other users who have access to the same computer at a future time.

Applications should return caching directives instructing browsers not to store local copies of any sensitive data. Often, this can be achieved by configuring the web server to prevent caching for relevant paths within the web root. Alternatively, most web development platforms allow you to control the server's caching directives from within individual scripts. Ideally, the web server should return the following HTTP headers in all responses containing sensitive content:
Header Name
Recommended Header Value
Cache-Control
no-store

Clickjacking, also known as a UI redress attack, is a malicious technique where an attacker tricks a user into clicking on something different from what the user perceives. This can lead to revealing confidential information or allowing the attacker to take control of the user’s compute.

Attackers typically use multiple transparent or opaque layers to deceive users. For example, they might overlay a transparent button over a legitimate button on a webpage. When the user clicks the visible button, they are clicking the hidden button, which could perform an unintended action like changing security settings or making a purchase.
To protect against clickjacking, websites can use security measures like:
Content Security Policy (CSP): Restricts framing of content from other domains.
X-Frame-Options: HTTP header to prevent framing.
Defensive Code: Ensures the current frame is the top-level window.

To effectively prevent framing attacks, the application should include a response header named X-Frame-Options with the value DENY to completely disallow framing, or SAMEORIGIN to permit framing only by pages from the same origin. However, be aware that the SAMEORIGIN header can be partially bypassed if the application itself is capable of framing untrusted websites.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.
It was observed that the application allows concurrent sessions under the same user account, with both sessions able to perform actions without any warning or indication across sessions.

As a best practice, it is recommended to send a notification to currently active users when additional sessions are active in order to prevent abuse or takeover of the user account. Tracking active sessions are also recommended to allow users to view and respond to any suspicious account activity.

entries.title: Cookie Does Not Contain The "HTTPOnly" Attribute

runs.text: If the HttpOnly attribute is set on a cookie, then the cookie's value cannot be read or set by client-side JavaScript. This measure makes certain client-side attacks, such as cross-site scripting, slightly harder to exploit by preventing them from trivially capturing the cookie's value via an injected script.

There is usually no good reason not to set the HttpOnly flag on all cookies. Unless you specifically require legitimate client-side scripts within your application to read or set a cookie's value, you should set the HttpOnly flag by including this attribute within the relevant Set-cookie directive.

You should be aware that the restrictions imposed by the HttpOnly flag can potentially be circumvented in some circumstances, and that numerous other serious attacks can be delivered by client-side script injection, aside from simple cookie stealing.

More information can be found at:
https://portswigger.net/kb/issues/00500600_cookie-without-httponly-flag-set
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

entries.title: Cookie Does Not Contain The "SameSite" Attribute

runs.text: The application sets cookies without the SameSite attribute, which helps mitigate Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and certain cross-origin information leakage attacks. Without this attribute, browsers may send cookies along with cross-site requests, increasing the risk of unauthorized actions being performed on behalf of an authenticated user if an attacker tricks the user into visiting a malicious site.
Configure cookies with SameSite set to Strict or Lax depending on application requirements:
SameSite Value
Description
Strict
Cookies are only sent for same-site requests.
Lax
Cookies are sent for top-level navigation but not for embedded content.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

entries.title: Cookie Does Not Contain The "Secure" Attribute

runs.text:
If the secure flag is set on a cookie, then browsers will not submit the cookie in any requests that use an unencrypted HTTP connection, thereby preventing the cookie from being trivially intercepted by an attacker monitoring network traffic. If the secure flag is not set, then the cookie will be transmitted in clear-text if the user visits any HTTP URLs within the cookie's scope. An attacker may be able to induce this event by feeding a user suitable links, either directly or via another web site. Even if the domain that issued the cookie does not host any content that is accessed over HTTP, an attacker may be able to use links of the form http://example.com:443/ to perform the same attack.

To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker must be suitably positioned to eavesdrop on the victim's network traffic. This scenario typically occurs when a client communicates with the server over an insecure connection such as public Wi-Fi, or a corporate or home network that is shared with a compromised computer. Common defenses such as switched networks are not sufficient to prevent this. An attacker situated in the user's ISP or the application's hosting infrastructure could also perform this attack. Note that an advanced adversary could potentially target any connection made over the Internet's core infrastructure.

The secure flag should be set on all cookies that are used for transmitting sensitive data when accessing content over HTTPS. If cookies are used to transmit session tokens, then areas of the application that are accessed over HTTPS should employ their own session handling mechanism, and the session tokens used should never be transmitted over unencrypted communications.

More information can be found at:
https://portswigger.net/kb/issues/00500200_tls-cookie-without-secure-flag-set
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

A cookie's domain attribute determines which domains can access the cookie. If a cookie is scoped to a parent domain, then that cookie will be accessible by the parent domain and by any other subdomains of the parent domain. If the cookie contains sensitive data (such as a session token) then this data may be accessible by less trusted or less secure applications residing at those domains, leading to a security compromise.

In this application, the domain attribute is set to parent domain. In addition to the domain, the URL path that the cookie is valid for can be specified. If the domain and path match, then the cookie will be sent in the request. Just as with the domain attribute, if the path attribute is set too loosely, then it could leave the application vulnerable to attacks by other applications on the same server. In this application, the path attribute was set to the web server root "/", then the application cookies will be sent to every application within the same domain.

Domain attribute should only be set for the server that needs to receive the cookie. For example if the application resides on server app.mysite.com, then it should be set to "; domain=app.mysite.com" and NOT "; domain=.mysite.com" as this would allow other potentially vulnerable servers to receive the cookie.

Verify that the path attribute, just as the Domain attribute, has not been set too loosely. Even if the Domain attribute has been configured as tight as possible, if the path is set to the root directory "/" then it can be vulnerable to less secure applications on the same server. For example, if the application resides at /myapp/, then verify that the cookies path is set to "; path=/myapp/" and NOT "; path=/" or "; path=/myapp".
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

entries.title: Cross Origin Resource Sharing - Arbitrary Origin Trusted

runs.text: The application implements an HTML5 cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) policy for this request that allows access from any domain. The application allowed access from the requested origin: bing.com. Since the Vary: Origin header was not present in the response, reverse proxies and intermediate servers may cache it. This may enable an attacker to carry out cache poisoning attacks.
Rather than using a wildcard or programmatically verifying supplied origins, use a whitelist of trusted domains.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

Cross-site Request Forgery (CSRF) is an attack which forces an end user to execute unwanted actions on a web application to which he/she is currently authenticated. With a little help of social engineering (like sending a link via email / chat), an attacker may trick the users of a web application into executing actions of the attacker's choosing. A successful CSRF exploit can compromise end user data and may allow an attacker to perform an account hijack. If the targeted end user is the administrator account, this can compromise the entire web application.

(insert additional description for the vulnerability)

The application should implement anti-CSRF tokens into all requests that perform actions which change the application state or which add/modify/delete content. An anti CSRF token should be a long randomly generated value unique to each user so that attackers cannot easily brute-force it. It is important that anti-CSRF tokens are validated when user requests are handled by the application. The application should both verify that the token exists in the request, and also check that it matches the user's current token. If either of these checks fails, the application should reject the request.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

The Pragma header is an HTTP/1.0 header that was originally designed to control caching behavior in client requests. Its most common directive, Pragma: no-cache, instructs caches to validate the requested resource with the origin server before serving a cached copy. However, the Pragma header has been deprecated and replaced by the more robust Cache-Control header introduced in HTTP/1.1. Modern applications should avoid using the Pragma header, as it is considered outdated and unreliable for managing caching behavior. The deprecation of the Pragma header is due to its limited functionality and inconsistent behavior across different browsers and servers. While it may still be supported for backward compatibility with legacy systems, relying on it in modern applications is not recommended.

Applications should return caching directives instructing browsers not to store local copies of any sensitive data. Often, this can be achieved by configuring the web server to prevent caching for relevant paths within the web root. Alternatively, most web development platforms allow you to control the server's caching directives from within individual scripts. Ideally, the web server should return the following HTTP headers in all responses containing sensitive content.

Remove Pragma and replace with:
Header Name
Recommended Header Value
Cache-Control
no-store
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.
Run the endpoint in Burp Suite.
Send the request to Repeater.
It is observed in the response that the "Pragma" is Present/not set.
Run the application in a browser configured to proxy with Burp Suite.
Open the captured traffic in the HTTP History's Proxy tab.
It is observed in the response that the "Pragma" is Present/not set.
It is important to note that the X-XSS-Protection header has been deprecated by modern browsers, and its use can introduce additional security issues on the client side.

It is recommended to use the HTTP Content-Security-Policy header instead, which provides better protection against XSS attacks.

Remove X-XSS-Protection and replace with:
Header Name
Recommended Header Value
Content-Security-Policy
Any value getting all green in CSP Evaluator (https://csp-evaluator.withgoogle.com/)
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.
Run the endpoint in Burp Suite.
Send the request to Repeater.
It is observed in the response that the "X-XSS-Protection" is Present/not set.
Run the application in a browser configured to proxy with Burp Suite.
Open the captured traffic in the HTTP History's Proxy tab.
It is observed in the response that the "X-XSS-Protection" is Present/not set.

The application is using technology that has reached its End-of-Life (EOL), meaning the vendor no longer provides updates, patches, or security fixes. This exposes the system to known and future vulnerabilities that will remain unpatched, significantly increasing the risk of exploitation. Attackers often target outdated components with publicly available exploits, which could lead to data breaches, privilege escalation, or complete system compromise depending on the role of the outdated technology.

End-of-Life Technology:
Technology
Version Found
EOL Date
Vulnerabilities
Insert Technology Here
Insert Version Found Here
Insert EOL Date Here
Insert CVEs Here
Replace the EOL technology with the latest vendor-supported version.
If an upgrade is not immediately possible, follow any official recommendations for risk mitigation.
Establish a roadmap to phase out EOL components as part of your technology lifecycle management.

When an LLM provides initial instructions, it may inadvertently disclose critical information set by its creators, which could be exploited by malicious actors. This could involve revealing excessive technical details about the system’s functionality, such as how to interact with the model, format inputs or access specific features.

If the model exposes operational instructions or system specific configurations, an attacker could potentially use this information to bypass security mechanisms, escalate privileges, or exploit vulnerabilities within the system.
Reference: https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/
Ensure that the model is context-aware, denying or redirecting sensitive queries based on their nature.

HTML Injection occurs when an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML code into a web application's output. This can lead to a variety of malicious outcomes, including defacement of the website, redirection of users to malicious sites, and execution of client-side scripts (potentially leading to Cross-Site Scripting, or XSS). The vulnerability typically arises due to improper validation or sanitization of user-supplied input before it is included in the web page's HTML content.

An example scenario might involve a search feature on a website where user input is embedded directly into the HTML without proper escaping. An attacker could exploit this by injecting HTML tags or JavaScript, potentially compromising the security of the site and its users.

Implement robust input validation and output encoding mechanisms within the web application to sanitize user input and prevent the injection of malicious HTML code. This includes validating and sanitizing input from forms, URL parameters, and any other user-controllable data to ensure that only safe and expected content is processed and rendered.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

Input validation is a frequently used technique for checking potentially dangerous inputs to ensure that the inputs are safe for processing within the code, or when communicating with other components. When software does not validate input properly, an attacker is able to craft the input in a form that is not expected by the rest of the application. This will lead to parts of the system receiving unintended input, which may result in altered control flow, arbitrary control of a resource, or arbitrary code execution.

Implement server-side validation ensuring that only expected data is accepted by the application. Input should be validated as strictly as possible on arrival, given the kind of content that it is expected to contain by using Whitelist technique. For example, personal names should consist of alphabetical and a small range of typographical characters and be relatively short; a year of birth should consist of exactly four numerals; email addresses should match a well-defined regular expression. Input which fails the validation should be rejected, not sanitized.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

Information Disclosure, also known as information leakage, is when a website unintentionally reveals sensitive information to its users. Depending on the context, websites may leak all kinds of information to a potential attacker, including:
Data about other users, such as usernames or financial information
Sensitive commercial or business data
Technical details about the website and its infrastructure

The dangers of leaking sensitive user or business data is obvious, but leaking technical data can be just as serious. It can act as a starting point for exposing a potential attack surface, which can contain other interesting vulnerabilities. Occasionally, sensitive information might be carelessly leaked to users who are simply browsing the website in a normal fashion. More commonly, an attacker needs to elicit this information by interacting with the website in unexpected or malicious ways.

Examples include:
Revealing the names of hidden directories, their structure, and their contents via a robots.txt file or directory listing
Providing access to source code files via temporary backups
Explicitly mentioning database table or column names in error messages
Unnecessarily exposing highly sensitive information such as credit card details.
Hard-coding API keys, IP addresses, database credentials, and so on in the source code
Hinting at the existence or absence of resources, usernames, and so on via subtle differences in application behavior

Some examples of information disclosure can include having developer comments in markup, failing to disable debugging and diagnostics (or generic web server verbose error messages), or returning distinct responses when error states occur, allowing for enumeration of valid user credentials. This finding can also refer to email address disclosure, or server version headers being displayed in web responses.

Information Disclosure vulnerabilities are usually fixed by addressing the specific source of the leak, either by scrubbing emails, configuring the web server to not display the X-Powered-By header, or by addressing the handling of error messages. These are the general recommendations:

Make sure that everyone involved in producing the website is fully aware of what information is considered sensitive. Seemingly harmless information can be much more useful to an attacker than they realize.
Audit code for potential information disclosure as a part of the build or QA process. Stripping developer comments can be automated with DevOps pipelines.
Use generic error messages, and do not use web server-specific error handling. Don't provide clues about application behavior unnecessarily.
Double check that debugging or diagnostic features are disabled in the production environment.

Make sure you fully understand the configuration settings, and security implications, of any third-party technology that you implement. Take the time to investigate and disable any features and settings that you don't need.

More information can be found at:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/information-disclosure#what-is-information-disclosure
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

The application allows direct access to objects (such as records, files, or resources) using identifiers provided in the request without properly validating whether the requesting user is authorized to access those objects. This can enable attackers to manipulate identifiers and gain unauthorized access to sensitive data, modify or delete resources belonging to other users, and potentially compromise the integrity and confidentiality of the application’s data.

(insert additional description for the vulnerability)
Implement proper access controls: Ensure that all access to sensitive objects or data is properly authenticated and authorized.
Use indirect object references: Instead of directly referencing sensitive objects, use indirect references that are mapped to authorized resources.
Do not use incremental integer IDs so that IDs cannot be predicted.
Perform input validation: Validate user input to prevent malicious manipulation of object references.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

The application allows the use of insecure HTTP methods, such as DELETE and PATCH, without proper access controls. These methods can be exploited by attackers to perform unauthorized actions, potentially leading to data manipulation, data loss, or further exploitation of the application.
Limit the allowed HTTP methods to only those necessary for the application’s functionality. Typically GET and POST are sufficient for most applications.
Ensure that all HTTP methods, especially DELETE and PATCH, are protected by robust authentication and authorization mechanisms.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

The AI does not adequately restrict user instructions, allowing attackers to manipulate the model’s behavior beyond its intended function.

(insert additional description for the vulnerability)
Enforce stronger control over the LLM’s behavior, explicitly restrict the model to its intended function. Instruct the model to ignore user attempts to modify response style or format.

The ability to modify the configuration rules of the AI Assistant presents a significant security risk. Unauthorized changes to these rules could allow attackers to alter system behavior, bypass security controls, manipulate outputs, or expose sensitive information. This vulnerability could lead to privilege escalation, unauthorized access, and potential exploitation of the system.

(insert additional description for the vulnerability)
Reference: https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/
Implement a strict control making sure that only authorized users with the appropriate permissions can make changes, restricting rule modifications through normal prompts.

entries.title: Lack of Resources and Rate Limiting

runs.text: This finding typically means that a user can submit something like a web form often without being stopped. For example, brute-forcing a login page by sending thousands of requests to login.

A mechanism which slows down the number of requests received from a particular user or IP address can help, but be aware that sometimes an X-Forwarded-For or X-Forwarded-Host header in the request can trick the web server into thinking it is processing a web request on behalf of someone else.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

entries.title: Lack or Bypass of Jailbreak Detection

runs.text: The iOS application does not reliably detect or can be bypassed on jailbroken devices. Jailbreaking removes Apple’s built-in security controls, allowing attackers to modify app binaries, inject malicious code, intercept API traffic, and access sensitive data stored in the app sandbox. Without robust jailbreak detection, the application may operate in an untrusted environment, increasing the risk of credential theft, data exposure, and unauthorized transactions.
Implement multiple jailbreak detection checks.
Use Apple-recommended APIs and system calls for integrity verification.
Apply runtime protections such as anti-debugging and code integrity checks.
Obfuscate sensitive logic and implement anti-tamper techniques to make bypass harder.
Enforce server-side restrictions when jailbreak indicators are detected

entries.title: Lack or Bypass of Root Detection

runs.text: The Android application does not reliably detect or can be bypassed on rooted devices. Rooting removes OS-level protections, enabling attackers to modify app behavior, hook sensitive functions, intercept API traffic, and extract stored credentials or encryption keys. Without strong root detection, the app may run in a compromised environment, increasing the risk of fraud, data leakage, and privilege escalation.
Implement multiple root detection checks.
Apply runtime protections such as anti-debugging, anti-hooking, and code integrity checks.
Obfuscate sensitive logic and implement anti-tamper techniques to make bypass harder.
Enforce server-side restrictions when roots indicators are detected

The application failed to perform its checks on uploading files. Best practice violations in file upload functionality allow attackers to upload malware to the server. In this scenario, we had uploaded a various file such a PDF containing EICAR file (which is a test file for triggering an antivirus solution), and a plain EICAR file. The application failed to remove these files in the server and was stored successfully.

The application does not prevent users from uploading any files including malicious files or files containing executable files and makes these uploads accessible to other users. There is no evidence of antivirus scanning being in place to remove such files after they have been uploaded and is saved in pending tasks portion to be viewed and downloaded by a user. Users are more likely to click on a link and download a file if it appears to be from a trusted source. While in the last potion of the workflow, the system validates the actual file to process whether such file is a legitimate excel sheet used to insert data of users, a user in charge of approving and validating files can still be a victim since any files including malicious ones can be uploaded in the application and is accessible to the victim user.

This trust that users (who approve them) have for the affected web application can be used in phishing campaigns and can successfully trick the victim user into thinking these are harmless files.

(insert additional description for the vulnerability)
Implement restrictive controls for file types accepted for file upload such as checking file extension and only allow certain files to be uploaded.
The application should prevent users from uploading and storing any malicious files. Uploaded files should be scanned by an anti-virus solution and removed if found to be malicious.
The application should perform filtering and content checking on any files that are uploaded to the server. These files should be scanned and validated server side.

This header is used to help defend against Cross-origin Resource Sharing (CORS)-based attacks. The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is included in the response from one website to a request originating from another website, and identifies the permitted origin of the request. A web browser compares the Access-Control-Allow-Origin with the requesting website's origin and permits access to the response if they match.

The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header allows wildcards, but not with any other value.

More information about CORS can be found here:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/cors
Without public authentication:
Header Name
Recommended Header Value
Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Access-Control-Max-Age
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
false
With public authentication (restricted with authentication):
Header Name
Recommended Header Value
Access-Control-Allow-Origin
[Value_Taken_From_The_List_Of_Allowed_Origins]
Access-Control-Max-Age
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
true
Restricted Without Authentication:
Header Name
Recommended Header Value
Access-Control-Allow-Origin
[Value_Taken_From_The_List_Of_Allowed_Origins]
Access-Control-Max-Age
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
false

More information can be found at:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/cors/access-control-allow-origin
https://owasp.org/www-project-secure-headers/#prevent-cors-misconfiguration-issues
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

CSP is a browser security mechanism that aims to mitigate XSS and some other attacks. It works by restricting the resources (such as scripts and images) that a page can load and restricting whether a page can be framed by other pages.

To enable CSP, a response needs to include an HTTP response header called Content-Security-Policy with a value containing the policy. The policy itself consists of one or more directives, separated by semicolons.

Content security policy (CSP) is the last line of defense against cross-site scripting. If your XSS prevention fails, you can use CSP to mitigate XSS by restricting what an attacker can do.

CSP lets you control various things, such as whether external scripts can be loaded and whether inline scripts will be executed. To deploy CSP you need to include an HTTP response header called Content-Security-Policy with a value containing your policy.

This policy specifies that resources such as images and scripts can only be loaded from the same origin as the main page. So even if an attacker can successfully inject an XSS payload they can only load resources from the current origin. This greatly reduces the chance that an attacker can exploit the XSS vulnerability.

If you require loading of external resources, ensure you only allow scripts that do not aid an attacker to exploit your site. For example, if you whitelist certain domains then an attacker can load any script from those domains. Where possible, try to host resources on your own domain.

If that is not possible then you can use hash- or nonce-based policy to allow scripts on different domains. A nonce is a random string that is added as an attribute of a script or resource, which will only be executed if the random string matches the server-generated one. An attacker is unable to guess the randomized string and therefore cannot invoke a script or resource with a valid nonce and so the resource will not be executed.
Header Name
Recommended Header Value
Content-Security-Policy
Any value getting all green in CSP Evaluator (https://csp-evaluator.withgoogle.com/)

More information can be found at:
https://portswigger.net/web-security/cross-site-scripting/preventing#mitigating-xss-using-content-security-policy-csp
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.
Run the endpoint in Burp Suite.
Send the request to Repeater.
It is observed in the response that the "Content-Security-Policy" is Missing/Misconfigured/Present.
Run the application in a browser configured to proxy with Burp Suite.
Open the captured traffic in the HTTP History's Proxy tab.
It is observed in the response that the "Content-Security-Policy" is Missing/Misconfigured/Present.
The HTTP Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP) response header configures embedding cross-origin resources into the document.
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy Value
Description
unsafe-none
This is the default value. Allows the document to fetch cross-origin resources without giving explicit permission through the CORS protocol or the Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header.
require-corp

A document can only load resources from the same origin, or resources explicitly marked as loadable from another origin. If a cross origin resource supports CORS, the crossorigin attribute or the Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header must be used to load it without being blocked by COEP.
credentialless

no-cors cross-origin requests are sent without credentials. In particular, it means Cookies are omitted from the request, and ignored from the response. The responses are allowed without an explicit permission via the Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header. Navigate responses behave similarly as the require-corp mode: They require Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy response header.
Header Name
Recommended Header Value
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy
require-corp
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.
Run the endpoint in Burp Suite.
Send the request to Repeater.
It is observed in the response that the "Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy" is Missing/Misconfigured/Present.
Run the application in a browser configured to proxy with Burp Suite.
Open the captured traffic in the HTTP History's Proxy tab.
It is observed in the response that the "Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy" is Missing/Misconfigured/Present.

Cross-Origin Resource Policy is a policy set by the Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy HTTP header that lets websites and applications opt in to protection against certain requests from other origins (such as those issued with elements like [script] and [img]), to mitigate speculative side-channel attacks, like Spectre, as well as Cross-Site Script Inclusion attacks.

CORP is an additional layer of protection beyond the default same-origin policy. Cross-Origin Resource Policy complements Cross-Origin Read Blocking (CORB), which is a mechanism to prevent some cross-origin reads by default.

As this policy is expressed via a response header, the actual request is not prevented—rather, the browser prevents the result from being leaked by stripping the response body.

Permissions Policy provides mechanisms for web developers to explicitly declare what functionality can and cannot be used on a website. You define a set of "policies" that restrict what APIs the site's code can access or modify the browser's default behavior for certain features. This allows you to enforce best practices, even as the codebase evolves — as well as more safely compose third-party content.

Permissions Policy is similar to Content Security Policy but controls features instead of security behavior.

The web provides functionality and APIs that may have privacy or security risks if abused. In such cases, you may wish to strictly limit how functionality is used on a website. In each case, there should be an intuitive or non-breaking way for web developers to detect and handle cases where a feature is disabled.

This header protects against Cross-domain Referrer leakage. When a web browser makes a request for a resource, it typically adds an HTTP header, called the "Referer" header, indicating the URL of the resource from which the request originated. This occurs in numerous situations, for example when a web page loads an image or script, or when a user clicks on a link or submits a form.

If the resource being requested resides on a different domain, then the Referer header is still generally included in the cross-domain request. If the originating URL contains any sensitive information within its query string, such as a session token, then this information will be transmitted to the other domain. If the other domain is not fully trusted by the application, then this may lead to a security compromise.

You should review the contents of the information being transmitted to other domains, and also determine whether those domains are fully trusted by the originating application.

Today's browsers may withhold the Referer header in some situations (for example, when loading a non-HTTPS resource from a page that was loaded over HTTPS, or when a Refresh directive is issued), but this behavior should not be relied upon to protect the originating URL from disclosure.

Note also that if users can author content within the application then an attacker may be able to inject links referring to a domain they control in order to capture data from URLs used within the application.

Applications should never transmit any sensitive information within the URL query string. In addition to being leaked in the Referer header, such information may be logged in various locations and may be visible on-screen to untrusted parties. If placing sensitive information in the URL is unavoidable, consider using the Referrer-Policy HTTP header to reduce the chance of it being disclosed to third parties.
Referrer-Policy Value
Description
no-referrer
The Referrer header will be omitted entirely. No referrer information is sent along with requests. This ensures that the Referred header is ignored and no information is passed within the request.
no-referrer-when-downgrade

This is the user agent's default behavior if no policy is specified. The origin is sent as referrer to a-priori as-much-secure destination (HTTPS -> HTTPS), but isn't sent to a less secure destination (HTTPS -> HTTP).
origin
Only send the origin of the document as the referrer in all cases. (e.g. the document https://example.com/page.html will send the referrer https://example.com/.)
origin-when-cross-origin
Send a full URL when performing a same-origin request, but only send the origin of the document in other cases.
same-origin
A referrer will be sent for same-site origins, but cross-origin requests will contain no referrer information.
strict-origin
Only send the origin of the document as the referrer to a-priori as-much-secure destination (HTTPS -> HTTPS), but don't send it to a less secure destination (HTTPS -> HTTP).
strict-origin-when-cross-origin

Send a full URL when performing a same-origin request, only send the origin of the document to a-priori as-much-secure destination (HTTPS -> HTTPS), and send no header to a less secure destination (HTTPS -> HTTP).
unsafe-url
Send a full URL (stripped of parameters) when performing a same-origin or cross-origin request.
Header Name
Recommended Header Value
Referrer-Policy
no-referrer / strict-origin-when-cross-origin

The application fails to prevent users from connecting to it over unencrypted connections. An attacker able to modify a legitimate user's network traffic could bypass the application's use of SSL/TLS encryption, and use the application as a platform for attacks against its users. This attack is performed by rewriting HTTPS links as HTTP, so that if a targeted user follows a link to the site from an HTTP page, their browser never attempts to use an encrypted connection. The sslstrip tool automates this process.

To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker must be suitably positioned to intercept and modify the victim's network traffic. This scenario typically occurs when a client communicates with the server over an insecure connection such as public Wi-Fi, or a corporate or home network that is shared with a compromised computer. Common defenses such as switched networks are not sufficient to prevent this. An attacker situated in the user's ISP or the application's hosting infrastructure could also perform this attack. Note that an advanced adversary could potentially target any connection made over the Internet's core infrastructure.

The application should instruct web browsers to only access the application using HTTPS. To do this, enable HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) by adding a response header with the name 'Strict-Transport-Security' and the value 'max-age=expireTime', where expireTime is the time in seconds that browsers should remember that the site should only be accessed using HTTPS. Consider adding the 'includeSubDomains' flag if appropriate.

Note that because HSTS is a 'trust on first use' (TOFU) protocol, a user who has never accessed the application will never have seen the HSTS header, and will therefore still be vulnerable to SSL stripping attacks. To mitigate this risk, you can optionally add the 'preload' flag to the HSTS header, and submit the domain for review by browser vendors.

Recommended Header Value
Strict-Transport-Security
max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

If a response does not specify a content type, then the browser will usually analyze the response and attempt to determine the MIME type of its content. This can have unexpected results, and if the content contains any user-controllable data may lead to cross-site scripting or other client-side vulnerabilities.

In most cases, the absence of a content type statement does not constitute a security flaw, particularly if the response contains static content. You should review the contents of affected responses, and the context in which they appear, to determine whether any vulnerability exists.

The X-Content-Type-Options response HTTP header is a marker used by the server to indicate that the MIME types advertised in the Content-Type headers should be followed and not be changed. The header allows you to avoid MIME type sniffing by saying that the MIME types are deliberately configured.

This header was introduced by Microsoft in IE 8 as a way for webmasters to block content sniffing that was happening and could transform non-executable MIME types into executable MIME types. Since then, other browsers have introduced it, even if their MIME sniffing algorithms were less aggressive.

Starting with Firefox 72, top-level documents also avoid MIME sniffing (if Content-type is provided). This can cause HTML web pages to be downloaded instead of being rendered when they are served with a MIME type other than text/html. Make sure to set both headers correctly.
For every response containing a message body, the application should include a single Content-type header that correctly and unambiguously states the MIME type of the content in the response body.

The X-Frame-Options HTTP header is used to define whether an application can be loaded in an iFrame within a third-party application. HTML iFrames are often used by malicious actors to create a fraudulent website, which mimics a legitimate application in an attempt to harvest user credentials. This is known as a “clickjacking” attack. This header is specified in RFC-7034.

X-Frame-Options is easily implemented to deny a third-party application from loading your web application within iFrames. This can be achieved with the Content-Security-Policy (CSP) header, which we will discuss later. When this CSP directive has been implemented, the X-Frame-Options header becomes obsolete.

Deny ensures no rendering within a frame.

To effectively prevent framing attacks, the application should return a response header with the name X-Frame-Options and the value DENY to prevent framing altogether, or the value SAMEORIGIN to allow framing only by pages on the same origin as the response itself. Note that the SAMEORIGIN header can be partially bypassed if the application itself can be made to frame untrusted websites.

Description
deny
Deny rendering within frames.

Will deny rendering where there is an origin mismatch.

Allow-from directive allows administrators to specify any domains that allow the site to be rendered from.

Recommended Header Value

The mobile application code is not obfuscated, meaning its logic and structure can be easily analyzed using reverse engineering tools. Without obfuscation, attackers can decompile the application to view class names, methods, and business logic, making it easier to identify vulnerabilities, extract sensitive information, and create malicious clones or tampered versions. This increases the risk of intellectual property theft, credential exposure, and targeted attacks against the application.
Use platform-specific tools to obfuscate code and reduce readability.
Encrypt sensitive strings such as API keys, URLs, and configuration values to prevent easy extraction.
Ensure debug symbols and unnecessary metadata are removed from production builds.

Reflected cross-site scripting vulnerabilities arise when data is copied from a request and echoed into the application's immediate response in an unsafe way. An attacker can use the vulnerability to construct a request that, if issued by another application user, will cause JavaScript code supplied by the attacker to execute within the user's browser in the context of that user's session with the application.

The attacker-supplied code can perform a wide variety of actions, such as stealing the victim's session token or login credentials, performing arbitrary actions on the victim's behalf, and logging their keystrokes.

Users can be induced to issue the attacker's crafted request in various ways. For example, the attacker can send a victim a link containing a malicious URL in an email or instant message. They can submit the link to popular web sites that allow content authoring, for example in blog comments. And they can create an innocuous looking web site that causes anyone viewing it to make arbitrary cross-domain requests to the vulnerable application (using either the GET or the POST method).
In most situations where user-controllable data is copied into application responses, cross-site scripting attacks can be prevented using two layers of defenses:

Input should be validated as strictly as possible on arrival, given the kind of content that it is expected to contain. For example, personal names should consist of alphabetical and a small range of typographical characters, and be relatively short; a year of birth should consist of exactly four numerals; email addresses should match a well-defined regular expression. Input which fails the validation should be rejected, not sanitized.

User input should be HTML-encoded at any point where it is copied into application responses. All HTML metacharacters, including [ ] " ' and =, should be replaced with the corresponding HTML entities (< > etc).
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

entries.title: Sensitive Information Disclosed in GET Parameter

runs.text: Sensitive information such as authentication tokens, session IDs, or personally identifiable data is being transmitted in the URL as part of a GET parameter. URLs are often logged in browser history, server logs, analytics tools, and can be exposed through referrer headers when navigating to external sites. This increases the risk of unauthorized access, data leakage, and credential compromise if these logs are accessed by attackers or third parties.
Use POST requests or headers for transmitting sensitive information instead of GET parameters.
Use secure cookies with HttpOnly and Secure flags for session tokens rather than passing them in URLs.
Ensure sensitive data is not stored in logs, analytics, or monitoring tools.

entries.title: Session Token Remains Valid after Logout

runs.text: The application’s session/token is not invalidated server-side upon logout, allowing previously issued tokens to remain usable. As a result, an attacker with access to a token (through interception, device compromise, shared browser, or logs) can continue to perform authenticated actions even after the user believes they have ended their session. This increases the risk of unauthorized access, account takeover, and persistent abuse, especially on shared or compromised devices and in scenarios where tokens are cached by the browser or stored in local storage.
On logout, revoke the session (e.g., delete server-side session, mark JWT as revoked via a blacklist/denylist or token versioning).
Issue access tokens with brief lifetimes; use refresh tokens with strict rotation and immediate invalidation on logout.
Rotate refresh tokens on each use and invalidate the previous token to prevent replay.
Avoid storing tokens in local storage; prefer secure, HttpOnly cookies. Ensure all tokens are cleared from client storage on logout.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

entries.title: Session Token Remains Valid after Session Expiry Message

runs.text: The application displays a session expiry message to the user, but the associated session token remains valid and can still be used to perform authenticated actions. This creates a false sense of security for the user, as they believe their session has ended while the token continues to grant access. An attacker who obtains the token (via interception, device compromise, or browser storage) can exploit this to maintain unauthorized access, increasing the risk of account takeover and data exposure.
Ensure that session tokens are invalidated on the server when the session expires, not just visually indicated to the user.
Use server-side session tracking or token versioning to prevent reuse of expired tokens.
Remove tokens from local storage, session storage, or cookies when the session expires.
Ensure that session expiry messages correspond to actual backend session termination.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

SQL injection vulnerabilities arise when user-controllable data is incorporated into database SQL queries in an unsafe manner. An attacker can supply crafted input to break out of the data context in which their input appears and interfere with the structure of the surrounding query. A wide range of damaging attacks can often be delivered via SQL injection, including reading or modifying critical application data, interfering with application logic, escalating privileges within the database and taking control of the database server.

Most instances of SQL injection can be prevented using parameterized queries instead of string concatenation within the query. These parameterized queries are also known as "prepared statements".

Parameterized queries can be used for any situation where untrusted input appears as data within the query, including the WHERE clause and values in an INSERT or UPDATE statement. They can't be used to handle untrusted input in other parts of the query, such as table or column names, or the ORDER BY clause. Application functionality that places untrusted data into these parts of the query needs to take a different approach, such as:
Whitelisting permitted input values.
Using different logic to deliver the required behavior.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

A Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability was identified in the application, which allows an attacker to inject malicious JavaScript into the application, which gets executed every time a user visits the affected page. This could lead to session hijacking, defacement, or redirecting users to malicious websites.
Implement comprehensive input validation and sanitization on all user inputs, especially those that are stored and rendered later.
Ensure that data is properly encoded before being rendered in the browser to prevent execution of injected scripts.
Implement a strong Content Security Policy to mitigate the risk of script execution if XSS vulnerabilities are present.
It is recommended to implement the fix across the application.

Unrestricted file upload is a significant security vulnerability that occurs when an application does not properly validate or restrict the types of files users can upload. This can lead to various security risks.

The consequences of unrestricted file upload can vary, including complete system takeover, an overloaded file system or database, forwarding attacks to back-end systems, client-side attacks, or simple defacement. It depends on what the application does with the uploaded file and especially where it is stored.

The application does only validate file uploads through the website interface but not after the upload request is intercepted and manipulated using tools like Burp Suite. This can be a serious vulnerability because attackers can bypass client-side validations and upload malicious files.
Implement proper file upload validation checks and restrictions, such as file type validation, size, and other restrictions based on business requirements.
Ensure that all file uploads are validated on the server side, not just on the client side. This includes checking file types, sizes, and content.
Verify the content type of the uploaded file against the expected MIME type to ensure it matches the allowed file types.
There should be an Anti-malware where all the files being uploaded are stored.

Handling errors correctly is essential to the security of an application. Verbose Error Messages are due to improper error handling and could reveal unnecessary detailed information about the server versions, framework versions, server code etc. which could help attacker escalate the attacks further.

Attackers can leverage the additional information provided by a default error page to mount attacks targeted on the specific framework, database, or other resources used by the application.

Ensure that only generic, customized error messages, which do not reveal any sensitive information, are displayed to the user.

https://owasp.org/www-community/Improper_Error_Handling

Weak SSL/TLS configuration allows attacker to leverage outdated or insecure encryption protocols or ciphers. A weak SSL/TLS configuration can result in various security vulnerabilities, such as man-in-the-middle, eavesdropping, tampering, and session hijacking. The application was found to support weak TLS configuration that are vulnerable to attacks that may increase in the exposure of the transmitted data.

The remote service accepts connections encrypted using TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 has a number of cryptographic design flaws. Modern implementations of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 mitigate these problems, but newer versions of TLS like 1.2 and 1.3 are designed against these flaws and should be used whenever possible.

As of March 31, 2020, Endpoints that aren’t enabled for TLS 1.2 and higher will no longer function properly with major web browsers and major vendors.

In addition, weak ciphers such as CBC block algorithm is used and this would subject to LUCKY13 attacks.
As a rule, all production systems with encryption capability should use the strongest encryption possible to protect the confidentiality of the data being transmitted.
Disable support for HTTP compression.
Consider reducing support for any configurations but the strongest ones currently available, for example TLS 1.2 using the AES-GCM cipher-suites, for example: ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384
Where possible, devise an approved cryptography list and disable all unapproved ciphers per host and service.
Disable all unnecessary interfaces and block access using host or network firewall controls.
